content: Hi everyone, great to have you all here — thanks for giving up your time today. We're going to spend about 45 minutes just talking, and the whole thing will be recorded for research purposes, so if that's okay with you, we'll get going. Before we do, just a few things to flag. There are no right or wrong answers here — genuinely, I'm not looking for any particular response, and whatever you actually think or do in real life is way more useful to me than anything polished or carefully worded. So try not to overthink it, just speak freely. And this is a conversation, not an interview — so if something someone else says connects with your experience, just jump in. You don't need to wait your turn, though you can if you want. The one thing I'd ask is just to be respectful of each other and keep your answers reasonably brief so everyone gets a chance to talk. Okay — let's start. If you could go around and say your name and where in the UK you're coming from today, that'd be great.
Right, yeah. I'm Amir, I'm 20, from Birmingham — well, the West Midlands properly. Been here my whole life, innit. That's me.
I'm David, I'm 27, from Glasgow. Been here most of my life as well, so yeah — urban Scotland through and through really.
Yeah, cheers. I'm Ibrahim, I'm 24, from the North East — urban area. Been here most of my life as well, so yeah, same kind of thing really. Looking forward to talking about all this.
Yeah, alright. I'm Isaiah, 26, from Yorkshire — urban bit up here. Been around the area most of my life, so yeah, same as you lot really. Cool to meet everyone.

Yeah, cheers. I'm Will, I'm 29, from rural Scotland — so a bit different from you lot, I suppose. Village area, nowhere near a city really. Been here my whole life as well, but it's a completely different setup to what you're all describing, I'd imagine. Anyway, looking forward to seeing where this goes.

Great, cheers everyone — Amir, David, Ibrahim, Isaiah, Will. So we've got a bit of a spread across the UK, urban and rural, which is interesting. Right, let's get into it. First question — and be as specific as you like here: what's your favourite place in your city, town, wherever you are, to spend time with your male friends? Why that place?

Oh, yeah — so for me it's probably the high street area, like round town. There's loads of restaurants and that, you know, places to grab food. We'll go to the gym sometimes too, which is just nearby. But honestly, most of the time we're just eating out somewhere, getting a bit of food, chatting. Could be a curry place, could be a chicken shop, doesn't really matter. Just somewhere we can sit down and have a laugh without it being too formal or anything. That's kind of it, really.

Yeah, that's fair — Glasgow's got that same thing going on, to be honest. Loads of spots on Sauchiehall Street and round there, you know? Pizza places, kebab shops, all that. We do the same thing — just grab food somewhere casual and hang about. 

Though I'd say Glasgow's got a bit of its own character with it, if that makes sense. Like, there's definitely that high street vibe Amir's talking about, but we've also got a fair few independent spots that have popped up over the years. Not trying to sound like I'm bigging up the city or anything, but it's got its own thing going on.

And yeah, the gym thing — that's pretty common round here as well. Seems like all the urban lads are doing similar stuff really, just different postcodes. What about you lot down south — Yorkshire and that?

Yeah, we've got that independent thing too, actually — like the Balti Quarter in Birmingham, that's kind of a big deal. Loads of proper curry restaurants, not chain stuff, you know? That's where we'll go sometimes. It's got more of a vibe than just going to Nando's or whatever for the thousandth time. But then you've got the chains as well, which is handy when you can't be bothered to travel far or you just want something quick.

I get what you mean about Glasgow having its own character though. It's the same with Brum, I reckon — there's stuff that's just... ours. But yeah, the gym thing is definitely universal with the lads I know.

Fair point about the independent spots — that's the kind of thing that does make a difference, isn't it? Not just chains all the way down.

But Will, what about you? You said it's quite different where you are. Are you even getting places like that to go to, or is it more of a case of having to travel a bit to find anything decent?

Yeah, we've got similar stuff in Leeds, to be fair. There's proper independent restaurants and that scattered about — not just chains everywhere. You can find decent places if you know where to look. The city centre's got a lot going on, and then there's bits outside that have their own thing.

Gym's the same as you lot though, yeah. That's pretty standard. And like, we'll do the food thing — grab something casual, sit around. Doesn't have to be fancy.

But I reckon it depends where you are in Yorkshire as well. Leeds is alright for that stuff, but I'd imagine if you're in a smaller town round here it's a bit different. Will, is it proper limited where you are then, or...?
Will, sounds like everyone's curious — over to you.

Yeah, so it's... it's quite different, to be honest. We don't really have that high street thing going on in the same way. Like, there's a wee pub in the village, that's kind of the hub for most people, and then if we want to do something a bit different we'd probably drive to the nearest town — but that's a fair bit away, so it's not something you do on a whim, you know?

The gym thing doesn't really happen where I am either. Some lads might have a home setup or go to the nearest leisure centre in town, but it's not the same casual thing as what you're all describing where you can just nip down the road. 

So when me and my mates hang about, it's more... we'll meet up at the pub, or someone's house, or we'll go for a walk or something outdoors. That's more just how it works round here. We're not really grabbing food at different spots every weekend or anything like that. It's more settled, I suppose — same few places, same routine. But honestly, I don't feel like we're missing out or anything. It's just how it is.
Cheers Will — that's a really different picture. Ibrahim, what about you — what's it like in London for that kind of thing?

Actually, I'm not in London — I'm up in the North East, so it's a bit more like what you lot are describing than Will's situation, but maybe not quite as much going on as the big cities, you know?

We've got decent enough spots on the high street, takeaways and that. Chicken shops, curry places, Chinese — it's all there. The gym's definitely a thing too. But I'd say it's not quite as mad with independent restaurants and all that as Birmingham or Leeds sounds. We do the same thing though — just grab food somewhere casual, have a laugh. That's kind of the standard, innit. 

I think the thing is, even if it's not as varied as what you lot have got, there's still enough that you can just meet up somewhere easy without it being a big production. It's workable.

Cheers Ibrahim — so we've got quite a range here, from Will's village pub to London, North East, Leeds, Birmingham, Glasgow. Interesting that the gym keeps coming up across all the urban ones. Let's build on that a bit — I want to ask something a bit more specific now: how do you actually decide what to eat, day to day? Like what goes into that decision for you?

Yeah, so for me it's... it's quite practical, I think. Like, it's not really a choice thing in the way you lot might be talking about it. It's more — what have I got in the house, what's available locally, and what fits with what I'm doing that day.

So during the week, I'll plan a bit ahead because if I need something specific, I can't just pop down to a shop five minutes away like you can. I might do a shop once a week or every couple of weeks, depending, and then I'm working with what I've got. Bit of chicken, some red meat, fish if I've managed to get to the supermarket — that kind of thing. Eggs, dairy, whatever. It's just... what makes sense with what I've got planned and what's available.

It's not really about "oh, I fancy that" on the day and then going out to get it. That's just not how it works here. You've got to think ahead a bit more. So the decision's made more when you're doing your shopping, really. What am I going to need over the next week or two?

I mean, it works fine — I don't feel like I'm missing anything. But it is a different way of thinking about it compared to what you're all describing, where you can just decide on the day and go somewhere.

Yeah, that makes sense — planning ahead because you've got to. But honestly, for me it's kind of the opposite. Like, I don't really plan it out like that. Most days I'll just decide when I'm hungry, you know? Oh, I fancy a bit of chicken tonight, or a curry, or whatever — and then I'll just go grab it because there's stuff nearby.

But I think what actually shapes my choice is — and I'm not gonna pretend it's not — is that I eat meat. Like, that's just what I go for. If I'm deciding between places on the day, I'm thinking, where can I get a decent bit of meat, innit? A good chicken shop, a kebab place, somewhere that does proper steaks. That's kind of the default for me.

I don't really think about it as a conscious thing most of the time, but if I'm honest, that's what narrows it down. Not just what's available — but what I actually want, and that tends to be meat-based. So the spontaneity is there because I can just go out and pick somewhere, but the choice isn't as open as it might sound, if that makes sense. It's meat first, then figure out where.

Yeah, that's fair — I'm the same with meat, to be honest. It's just what I eat. But I think the difference for me is, I've already made that decision before I even get to the point where you're deciding on the day, you know? Because I'm planning the week ahead, I'm already thinking — right, I'll get some chicken for Tuesday, some beef for Thursday, whatever. It's sorted.

So it's still the default for me, same as you, but it happens at a different stage because of where I am. You're spontaneous about it because you can be — you've got the shops there, you can just go get it. For me, it's more built into the routine from the start.

But yeah, I get what you're saying about it being the default without really thinking about it. That's just... that's what you eat, isn't it? I don't sit down and go through options every time. It's just what makes sense.

Yeah, but I think there's still something different about it though, even if it's the same default at the end of the day. Like, you're right that it's what I eat without thinking — but that's because I've actually chosen it, you know? Not just passively fallen into it.

Like, I could go to a veggie place if I wanted to. There's loads of them about. But I don't, because I don't fancy it. I prefer meat. It's a habit, yeah, but it's also just... what I like. The taste, the way it fills you up, all that. So when I'm deciding on the day, I'm not just defaulting because there's no other option — I'm defaulting because that's what I actually want.

Whereas what you're saying sounds like it's more just... that's what you've got, that's what fits with the week, so that's what it is. Which fair enough, totally different situation. But I think for me it's worth being honest about — it's not just passive, it's actually a preference thing. I've never been that bothered about trying something different because this is what I like.

No, I hear you — but I think I'm not explaining it right. It's not like I'm just passively accepting what's available either. I do choose meat. I like it — the taste, the way it fills you up, like you said. That's not different from you.

The thing is, I've still made that choice. It's just... I make it when I'm doing my shopping, not when I'm hungry on the day. But it's still a choice, you know? I'm not just eating meat because it's there and there's nothing else. I'm eating meat because that's what I want to eat. It just happens in a different way because of where I live.

So yeah, it's a preference thing for me too. I'm not defaulting because I've got no other option — I'm doing it because that's what I actually prefer. It's just that my version of deciding happens a week or two ahead instead of on the spot. But the preference bit is the same.

So Will and Ibrahim are both landing in a similar place — meat as a genuine preference, not just what's there — even if the decision happens at different moments. What about the rest of you? How does that sit with how you think about it?

Yeah, I mean... I think for me it's a bit of both, to be honest. Like, I eat meat most of the time, yeah — chicken, bit of fish, that kind of thing. But I don't know if I'd say it's this strong preference thing where I'm sitting there thinking about it. It's more just... that's what I grab when I'm hungry, you know?

I could probably eat something else and be fine with it. I'm not bothered either way really. But when I'm deciding what to have, meat's just the default — there's a chicken shop round the corner, a kebab place, whatever. So that's what I go for. Not because I've thought it through and decided "no, meat's what I want," but just because it's there and easy and I haven't really thought about doing anything different.

I suppose that's a bit more like what you were saying, Will — it's just what happens. Not a massive preference thing, just... the default. But yeah, I do actually like it when I eat it. It's not like I'm forcing myself or anything. It's just not something I've spent much time thinking about, if that makes sense.

Yeah, I'm kind of with Isaiah on that, actually. Like, I eat meat — chicken, bit of red meat, fish and that. But I don't know if I sit down thinking about it as this big preference thing, you know? It's just... that's what you eat. That's what I've always eaten, that's what my mates eat, that's what's easiest to grab.

But I think — and this is the thing — I do actually like it. Like, the taste, it fills you up, it's satisfying. If I went without it, I'd probably miss it a bit. But whether that's because I genuinely prefer it or because it's just what I'm used to... I don't know, to be honest. I haven't really thought about it that much.

It's kind of like what Isaiah said — it's just the default without much thinking. But that doesn't mean I don't like it. It's just not something I've had to actively choose or defend or anything. It's just there.

Yeah, exactly. That's what I mean, like. You're not sitting there going "right, today I'm choosing meat because I prefer it" — it's just... you have it, you like how it tastes, and that's that. But then you can't really tell if you like it because it's actually better, or because you've just had it your whole life and that's what feels normal, you know?

I think the thing is, I've never really needed to question it. There's no reason to. It's not like I'm avoiding vegetables or anything — I'll eat them if they're there. But when I'm deciding what to have for dinner, meat's just the thing that comes to mind first. And I enjoy it when I eat it. But whether that's genuine preference or just... familiarity... I couldn't tell you honestly. 

Like, would I actually prefer a steak to something else if I'd grown up eating different stuff? Maybe. Maybe not. It's hard to say when you've never really tried anything different in that way.
David, we haven't heard from you yet on this one — how does it work for you?

Yeah, so... I think I'm a bit different from what you lot are saying, actually. Like, I eat meat, right — chicken, bit of beef, fish — but honestly I'm not that fussed about it either way. It's not something I've got strong feelings about.

I'll have it because it's there and it's easy, same as you lot. But if I didn't have meat one day and had something else instead, I'd be fine with that too. It's not like I'm craving it or thinking it's better than other stuff. It just... doesn't matter that much to me.

I think what you're both kind of dancing around — the preference thing versus just habit — I think that gets a bit overblown sometimes, to be honest. Like, I don't need to have this big conversation with myself about whether I "really" prefer meat or if I'm just used to it. It's just food. I eat it, I don't hate it, and that's enough.

What I do think is worth saying though — and this is maybe not relevant right now, but I reckon it will come up — is that I find it a bit weird when people tie meat eating to... I don't know, being a bloke or whatever. Like, that whole thing about "real men eat meat" or whatever you want to call it. That feels off to me. You're just eating something. It doesn't say anything about you.

But yeah, on the day-to-day thing — I'm just not that bothered about it either way.

Cheers David — and yeah, that gender thing is worth coming back to. Something to pick up in a bit. 

But something a few of you have touched on — Amir mentioned eating what your mates eat, David you implied a kind of group norm thing too. I'm curious how much the people around you actually shape what you eat — whether that's mates, family, whoever. Does that play into it much for any of you?

Yeah, I think that does come into it, actually — more than you might realize at first. Like, when you're going out with your mates, you're not gonna be the one person ordering something completely different from what everyone else is doing, are you? There's a bit of... I don't know, a social thing there.

But I think what's more interesting is the stuff you don't notice. Like, growing up, my family ate meat, so that was just normal. That's what you have at dinner. And then when you're out with your mates, they're doing the same thing, so it reinforces it. It becomes this invisible thing where you don't even think about it — not because you've decided it's the best option, but just because that's what everyone around you is doing.

I think that's fair enough, to be honest. That's how habits form. But I reckon where it gets a bit dodgy is when people start making out like that's some kind of... I don't know, statement about who you are as a person. Like, you're just eating what's normal in your group. That's not about being a bloke or being tough or any of that stuff. It's just what you grew up with and what your mates do.

So yeah, social influence definitely plays into it. But I don't think it needs to be dressed up as anything more than that.

Yeah, that invisible reinforcement thing David's describing — you just eat what your family ate, your mates do the same, and it never really becomes a decision — I think that's come through from a few of you in different ways. Good. 

So let's pick up on the thing David's mentioned a couple of times now, because I think it's actually the next question anyway. Does your gender influence what you eat? And I don't just mean in some abstract sense — I mean in practice, day to day, or in certain situations. Does being a man shape what you order, what you cook, what you'll admit to liking? Any of you?

I mean... yeah, I think there's something there, to be honest. Not like, in some obvious way where you're thinking about it. But like, when you're with your mates, there's definitely a vibe about certain things.

Like, I wouldn't really order a salad when I'm out with the lads, you know? Not because I think salad's rubbish or anything — sometimes a salad's nice. But there's just this... it feels a bit weird, doesn't it? You'd get a bit of stick for it, probably. Nothing massive, just like, a comment or whatever.

And with cooking at home, if I was cooking for my mates to come round, I wouldn't be making something light or whatever. You'd make like a big curry or a steak or loads of chicken — something that feels proper, that you'd feel confident serving. That's just what feels right in that situation.

I don't think it's like some massive thing or like I'm being oppressed or whatever. It's just... there's an unspoken thing, innit? About what fits and what doesn't. And meat's kind of in the fits category, and some other stuff isn't. It's more comfortable that way.

Amir's talking about something quite specific there — this sense that ordering a salad with the lads would just feel off, that there's a kind of unspoken thing about what fits. Does that land for anyone else, or does it play out differently where you are?

Yeah, I know exactly what you mean, Amir. And I think it's worth saying — it's not nothing, you know? Like, you're downplaying it a bit, saying it's not a massive thing, but it actually is. It shapes what you do.

I've definitely felt that. Like, if I'm out with the lads and everyone's ordering burgers or chicken or whatever, you're not gonna be the one person going "oh, I'll have the salad." There's just this... it's awkward, innit? Not because anyone's gonna give you a massive hard time necessarily, but because there's an assumption about what you should be doing, what's normal in that situation. And meat fits into that. It's the safe choice.

The thing is, I'm not even saying that's wrong or anything — I like meat anyway. But I think the point is, it's not just about preference or what you actually fancy. There's this social pressure thing happening that we're all kind of going along with without really talking about it. And it does shape what you order, what you'd cook, all that.

It's like, you can't even tell anymore whether you're doing something because you genuinely want to or because that's just what you're supposed to do in that situation. And I think that's worth being honest about, rather than just saying "oh, it's not a massive thing." It is. It's just quiet about it.

Yeah, nah, fair point — I was kind of downplaying it a bit. There is definitely something there. But I don't know if I'd say it's like, you can't tell what you want anymore, you know? Like, I do actually want the meat. That's not fake or anything.

It's more like... there's a social thing happening, yeah, but that doesn't mean I'm being forced into it or anything. I'm aware of it, but I'm also just doing what I actually want to do anyway. It happens to align with what fits socially, but that's not because I'm trapped by it — it's because I actually like eating meat.

I think the thing is, if I genuinely fancied a salad, I probably would order it and just deal with whatever. Like, it'd be a bit awkward, maybe, but it's not like I can't do it. It's just not what I want, so it doesn't come up.

The pressure's there, yeah. But I don't think it's controlling what I do, exactly. More like... it's just part of how things work, and most of the time I'm fine with that anyway.

But that's the thing though — you might not even know if you'd fancy a salad because you're not in a headspace where you'd consider it, right? Like, it's not that you're being forced or anything. I'm not saying that. But the pressure does something quieter than forcing — it just... narrows what you think about in the first place.

Like, you say if you genuinely fancied one you'd order it. But would you? Because you've kind of already decided, without really deciding, that's not what you do when you're with the lads. So you're not gonna spend much time thinking about it. You don't even get to the point of "do I fancy this?" because salad's already off the table in your head before you've looked at the menu.

I'm not saying you don't genuinely like meat — I do too. But I think what I was getting at is, it's hard to know how much of that is actual preference and how much is just... what you've always done, what everyone around you does, what feels safe socially. Because all that stuff gets mixed in together, doesn't it? You can't really untangle it.

And yeah, you probably could order a salad if you really wanted to. But the fact that you probably wouldn't, even if part of you wanted to — that's the pressure doing something. It's just not a dramatic thing. It's just there, shaping the choices without you really noticing.

Look, I get what you're saying, and like... maybe you're right that it narrows things a bit. But I don't know, man. I can't sit here and say "oh, I definitely want a salad but I'm too scared to order it." That's not honest. I just don't think about salad when I'm hungry with my mates. That might be because of the pressure, yeah, but it also might just be because I'm not into it.

The thing is, I can't prove either way, can I? I can't know what I'd want if the pressure wasn't there. But that doesn't mean the pressure is the main thing driving everything I do. Sometimes the social thing and what I actually want just... line up. And I think that's okay. That's just how it works.

Like, I'm aware there's pressure there — I'm not saying there isn't. But knowing something's there and being controlled by it are different things. I know salad's a bit of a weird order with the lads, and I'm fine with that, because I'm gonna order the meat anyway. That's not pressure winning — that's me just being... fine with how things work.

But yeah, you're making me think about it now, and I'm not gonna pretend I've got a perfect answer. It's messy, innit?

Amir's landed on 'it's messy' — and that feels honest. But you three haven't weighed in yet. Does that tension he and Ibrahim have been pulling at — between pressure and preference, what you'd actually want versus what's already kind of off the table — does it play out similarly for you, or differently?

Yeah, I think... I mean, listening to you lot, I'm realizing I haven't actually thought about it that hard, have I? Like, Amir's saying he just doesn't think about salad, and I get that — that's me too. But Ibrahim's got a point about not knowing if you don't think about it.

The thing is, I don't feel like there's this massive pressure on me or anything. Like, I can eat what I want. But then... I'm also never really in a situation where I'm questioning it, you know? I go out with the lads, everyone's getting meat-based stuff, I get meat-based stuff. It feels normal. It feels right. And I've never sat there and thought "actually, no, I want something different."

But I can't tell if that's because I've genuinely worked out that's what I prefer, or if it's just... inertia. Like, it's easier not to question it. There's no reason to. And yeah, maybe if I'd grown up in a different environment or if my mates were all different, I'd be doing something else. But that's not where I'm at.

I'm not gonna sit here and say the pressure's not there — it clearly is, like Amir said. But I also don't feel trapped by it or anything. It's more like... I've just never needed to push against it because the default works fine for me. Whether that means I actually prefer it or I just haven't bothered to find out... I genuinely don't know.

Yeah, that's fair. And I think that's actually the honest place to land, Isaiah — not knowing. Because you can't know without actually pushing against it, and there's no reason you should have to, you know?

I was maybe being a bit too hard on it before. Like, I was trying to say something about how the pressure shapes things even when you don't feel it directly. And I think that's true. But that's not the same as saying you're being controlled by it or that you don't actually like what you're eating. You probably do like it. Most of us probably do actually like meat.

The thing is though — and this is what I keep coming back to — you can't actually know the difference between "I like this because it's genuinely what I prefer" and "I like this because it's what I'm used to and what everyone around me does." And I think it's worth just... acknowledging that gap, you know? Not as some big dramatic thing, but just being honest that it's there.

Like, you haven't needed to push against it because it works. Fair enough. But that doesn't mean the pressure isn't there — it just means it doesn't feel like pressure because everything's already lined up that way. The pressure's in the lining up, not in the pushing back.

But yeah, I'm not saying you should go out and order a salad or anything. That's not the point. It's more just... being real about what's actually going on, I think.

Yeah, that... that actually makes sense. Like, when you put it that way — the pressure's in the lining up — that's different from what I was thinking. Because I was kind of going "well, nothing's forcing me," but you're right, that's not really the point, is it?

It's more like... everything's already arranged so I don't have to question it. So I don't. And then I'm just going along with that and calling it preference because it feels easy. But easy doesn't necessarily mean it's what I'd actually choose if I'd had to think about it properly.

I suppose what you're saying is, I've kind of let the default do the thinking for me. Which is fine — like, it works, I'm not unhappy with it. But I'm not being honest if I'm sitting here going "oh, it's just what I like" when really I've never actually tested whether I like it or I just like that it fits. That's different, innit?

I don't know if that changes anything about what I actually eat. Probably doesn't. But yeah, I think you're right that it's worth just... admitting that's what's happening, rather than pretending I've made some proper choice about it.
Will, you've been quiet on this one — does any of that ring true from where you are, or does it land differently?

Yeah, I think it's a bit different for me, honestly. Like, I hear what you lot are saying about the social thing — the lads, what everyone's doing, all that. And yeah, that's there. But where I am, it's not really about going out with mates and all ordering meat because that's what you do, you know? It's more just... that's what you eat. Full stop.

There's not really an alternative being presented in the first place, so there's no pressure in the way you're talking about. Like, no one's thinking "oh, should I have the salad or the meat?" because salad's not really... it's not a thing that comes up. You just eat what's available, what fits the week, what makes sense.

So I don't feel like I'm choosing between pressure and preference in the same way. It's more like, meat's just what you eat — that's your default before anything social even comes into it. It's not about fitting in with the lads or feeling weird about ordering something different. It's just... that's food, isn't it?

But I do get what Ibrahim's saying about not knowing if you actually prefer it because you've never had to question it. That bit does land with me. I eat meat, I like it fine, but I've also never really had reason to think about doing anything else. So yeah, maybe that's the same thing — the default doing the thinking for me. It's just happening at a different level because of where I live, not because of who I'm out with.

So across the four of you, there's something that keeps coming up — whether it's the lads all ordering the same thing, or just what's in front of you where you live, the choice kind of makes itself. You can all see the mechanism, even if you can't fully unpick whether you'd actually choose differently. But here's what I want to test: is there a specific food — not just salad in the abstract — something you can actually picture — that you'd genuinely feel uncomfortable eating in front of your mates? Not just 'wouldn't order it,' but it'd feel actually off, like it'd say something about you?

Yeah... I mean, okay. Like, a veggie burger or something. Or like, full vegetarian meal, you know? That would feel... yeah, that'd be weird. Not just a bit awkward — it'd actually feel like I'm making some kind of statement about myself or something.

Like, if I ordered a salad, it's one thing — bit odd, whatever. But if I was sat there with a veggie burger while everyone else had meat, or I was going on about being vegetarian, that feels different. That feels like I'm saying something, and I'm not sure I'd be comfortable with that, to be honest.

And I don't even know if it's because I actually think vegetarians are weird or something — I don't think that. But there's definitely something about it that feels... I dunno, like it's not just about the food anymore, you know? It becomes a thing about you. About your choices, your values, whatever. And that's where it gets uncomfortable, not just the food part.

So yeah, that's probably where the pressure is actually real for me, if I'm being honest. Not with salad. With stuff that feels like it's actually saying something.
